text.p: Pakistan's Jansher Khan begins the defence of his World Open squash title on Sunday knowing he has never fought a more important home campaign.
Jansher's avowed ambition is to reverse the record of his legendary compatriot Jahangir Khan who won six World Open titles and 10 British Open titles.

Jansher will be going for his sixth British title in Cardiff next April, but although his World Open tally already stands at a record seven, at 27 the lithe Pakistani world number one cannot afford to waste any future title opportunities.

Jansher won his first world title at the age of 18 when he swept out of Nawakilli, in the hills above Peshawar, to defeat Jahangir in the semifinals of the 1987 championship in Birmingham and then overturned Australia's Chris Dittmar in the final.
The decade that followed yielded 75 wins in major championships against only 42 defeats in all competition, but the effort involved now appears to be taking its toll.

He lost the Kong Kong final to Australia's Rodney Eyles, the world number two, back in September and, although he won both the Gesira Open in Egypt and the Qatar International in between, he lost again, to Australia's unseeded Craig Rowland, in last month's Tournament of Champions semifinals in New York.

Only two players, New Zealand's Ross Norman and Australia's Rodney Martin, have interrupted the control exerted by Jahangir and Jansher over the World Open title since 1981, and in all that time no foreign player has ever defeated them on Pakistani soil.
Were Jansher to come unstuck in the $130,000 event, the fans who took long enough to accept him as a replacement for the idolised Jahangir could force him to slink off back to Nawakilli.

Jansher was ill-prepared for the start of the PSA World Tour in Hong Kong, was caught seriously unprepared by Rowland in New York and withdrew suspiciously late from last week's German Masters in Nurtigen.
The draw there was remarkably similar to next week's World Open draw and offers him a probable second round encounter with the hottest player on the circuit at the moment...Jonathon Power of Canada.

Power became the first North American ever to win a major PSA World Tour event when he swept through a star studded field as a qualifier to frustrate Rowland in the final of the Tournament of Champions.

He then went to the German Masters as a qualifier and beat England's Simon Parke in the final after the world number 10 had recorded his own best sequence since returning from testicular cancer and chemotherapy.
If the defending champion contains Power in Karachi, his next opponent could well be Parke.

Eyles starts against Irish champion Derek Ryan, a notoriously troublesome opponent for even the best players, and is then scheduled to meet two more Australians, Anthony Hill and Brett Martin on his way to the final.
Martin is seeded three but, aged 33 and perhaps beginning to show the first signs of those years, he has failed to progress beyond the first round of the last three World Tour events.
